best-broadway-shows.intro:
November 2026 finds Broadway in a remarkably strong season, with critic scores averaging 86 out of 100 across the top-rated shows currently running. Whether you're a longtime theatergoer or planning your first visit to the Great White Way, the current lineup offers something genuinely worth your time and money.

Leading the pack is Hamilton, Lin-Manuel Miranda's genre-defining musical that continues to draw near-unanimous critical praise for its hip-hop score and inventive storytelling — a reminder that even years into its run, the production retains its power to surprise. Close behind, The Book of Mormon holds firm as one of Broadway's sharpest comedies, balancing irreverence with unexpected warmth in a way few musicals manage. Also generating significant buzz is Oh, Mary!, Cole Escola's wildly original take on Mary Todd Lincoln, which critics describe as one of the more singular comic performances to hit Broadway in recent memory.

Beyond those highlights, the current season reflects a notable range in tone and ambition. Downstate brings moral complexity and dramatic weight, while Maybe Happy Ending offers quiet emotional intimacy. Long-running spectacles like The Lion King and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child continue to demonstrate that theatrical craft, when executed at the highest level, doesn't fade with familiarity.

It's worth noting that critic scores, while a useful guide, don't capture every dimension of a theatergoing experience — personal taste, subject matter, and the energy of a live audience all play a role. The rankings here are based on aggregated professional reviews and reflect critical consensus rather than any single opinion.

If you're planning a visit to Broadway this November, browsing individual show pages will help you find the production that best fits what you're looking for.

best-broadway-plays.intro:

Leading the pack this month is Oh, Mary!, Cole Escola's wildly inventive comedy that reimagines Mary Todd Lincoln as a boozy, scene-stealing force of nature. Critics have responded with near-unanimous enthusiasm, making it one of the most talked-about productions of the season. Close behind is Downstate, Bruce Norris's unflinching drama that continues to challenge and unsettle audiences with its morally complex portrait of sex offenders navigating life after incarceration — the kind of work that sparks genuine conversation long after the curtain falls.

For theatergoers drawn to spectacle, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child remains one of the highest-rated productions currently running, with critics consistently singling out its stage magic and visual ambition as something genuinely difficult to replicate elsewhere.

Beyond these standouts, the current landscape rewards curiosity. Billy Crystal's one-man show blends humor and grief in ways critics find surprisingly affecting, while Here There Are Blueberries brings a Pulitzer-nominated Holocaust docudrama to the stage with quiet but lasting power. Jamie Lloyd's rave-infused production of Much Ado About Nothing, featuring Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell, offers a more divisive but energetically modern take on Shakespeare.

The average critic score across the top-rated shows sits at 78 out of 100, suggesting a season of genuine quality even where opinions diverge. Whether you're planning your first Broadway visit of the fall or looking to round out a busy theatergoing month, checking current availability and booking in advance is strongly recommended for the most in-demand productions.

Close behind, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child draws exceptional critical attention for its stage illusions and production ambition, earning the broadest base of critical consensus among the top-rated shows currently running — a distinction worth noting for families weighing their options.

Critics tend to find both shows entertaining without being particularly distinguished, though individual performances — particularly James Monroe Iglehart's Genie in Aladdin and Lorna Courtney's work in & Juliet — draw consistent praise. MJ The Musical and Wicked round out the higher-profile offerings, each generating divided critical opinion; both productions have genuine strengths, but neither achieves the cohesion that critics find in the top-rated entries.

Across the board, the average critic score sits at 74 out of 100, suggesting that while the season is solid, only a few productions genuinely distinguish themselves. Families with flexibility in their schedules and budgets are best served by checking the most current critic scores before booking, as casts and productions can shift and new reviews continue to accumulate throughout the season.

Equally compelling is Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club, Rebecca Frecknall's immersive reimagining that transformed its venue into an atmospheric experience critics found difficult to shake, earning an 88 from 26 reviewers. Meanwhile, Springsteen on Broadway drew on a different kind of intimacy, with Bruce Springsteen trading arena spectacle for something more personal and emotionally direct — a choice that resonated widely across 41 reviews.

What the 2021 season demonstrates, in retrospect, is a willingness to take risks: one-woman shows, unconventional staging, and deeply personal storytelling sit comfortably alongside beloved large-scale productions like The Lion King. The highest-rated shows from this year reward audiences who appreciate both spectacle and restraint in equal measure.

For anyone exploring these productions through revivals, touring productions, or recorded captures, the critical record from 2021 offers a reliable guide to where the most rewarding experiences can be found.

best-broadway-plays-2024.intro:
As November 2026 draws to a close, Broadway's 2024 season continues to demonstrate an exceptional standard of theatrical craft, with the top-rated shows averaging a remarkable 90 out of 100 across critic reviews. Whether you're a longtime theatergoer or planning your first visit to New York's stages, the current landscape offers something genuinely worth your time.

Among the season's most celebrated productions, War Horse stands at the top of the critical rankings, earning near-universal admiration for its breathtaking life-sized horse puppetry — a feat of stagecraft that critics consistently describe as magical. Equally commanding is Stereophonic, David Adjmi's immersive drama set inside a 1970s recording studio, which has accumulated the broadest critical consensus of any show this season and is widely regarded as one of the finest American plays in recent memory. People, Places and Things also merits close attention, with lead performer Denise Gough drawing career-defining notices for her raw and unflinching portrayal at the center of Duncan Macmillan's addiction drama.

Beyond these standouts, the highest-rated productions span a wide range of forms and ambitions — from the epic sweep of The Lehman Trilogy to the intimate biographical storytelling of Monsieur Chopin, and from the joyful energy of Million Dollar Quartet to the vital, emotionally resonant For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy. best-broadway-plays-2025.intro:
As November 2026 draws to a close, Broadway's 2025 season stands as a remarkable stretch for serious, ambitious theatrical work. Leading the field is Giant, which has drawn near-universal acclaim for John Lithgow's performance as Roald Dahl, cementing it as the critical standout of the season. Not far behind, Hannah Senesh brings the story of the WWII heroine to Broadway with what critics describe as transformative scenic design and a production of real emotional force. Angels in America, in Invictus Theatre's staging, has also earned strong notices, with reviewers pointing to pitch-perfect ensemble work and bold directorial choices as evidence that this canonical American play continues to reward fresh interpretation.

What is notable about this season as a whole is its range. Alongside large-scale revivals like Fiddler on the Roof and Angels in America, smaller and more unconventional productions — including Teatro La Plaza's Spanish-language Hamlet, performed by eight actors with Down syndrome, and Dave Harris's metatheatrical Tambo and Bones — have earned scores that place them firmly among the year's best-reviewed work. Critics appear to have responded to ambition and specificity wherever they found it, regardless of scale or familiarity of material.

The average critic score across the top-rated shows sits at 91 out of 100, suggesting a season that has delivered consistently at the highest level. For theatergoers still planning their November attendance, the breadth of strong options means there is no single obvious choice — which, by any measure, is a good problem to have.

best-broadway-plays-2026.intro:
November 2026 finds Broadway in a particularly thoughtful mood, with the season's highest-rated offerings leaning toward challenging, morally complex material rather than easy entertainment. The top-rated shows this month reflect a stage willing to ask difficult questions of its audiences.

Leading the pack is Downstate, Bruce Norris's unflinching drama that critics are calling a bold moral triumph. With an 87/100 critic score, it stands as the season's most acclaimed work — a testament to Broadway's capacity to engage with subjects that resist comfortable resolution. Close behind, Here There Are Blueberries brings Holocaust history to the stage in what reviewers describe as haunting and essential docudrama, earning praise for its commitment to difficult truths.

Not everything this season reaches for darkness. Billy Crystal's one-man show 860 earns strong notices for its masterful balance of humor and grief, and Jamie Lloyd's production of Much Ado About Nothing — featuring Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell — brings a rave-infused, confetti-drenched energy to Shakespeare that critics largely find electric and alive.

The season's average critic score of 76/100 suggests a solid if uneven landscape. Paranormal Activity demonstrates that genre stagecraft can earn genuine respect, while revivals of The Imaginary Invalid, Other Desert Cities, and A Few Good Men receive more divided responses, each finding admirers and detractors in roughly equal measure.

Taken together, the top-rated shows this November reflect a Broadway season that rewards adventurous theatergoing. Those looking to make the most of what's currently on offer would do well to prioritize the higher-scored productions before the winter holiday season shifts the theatrical calendar once again.
